nodes.text: Let $k\geq 3$. What is the maximum number of edges that a graph on $n$ vertices can contain if it does not have a $k$-regular subgraph? Is it $\ll n^{1+o(1)}$?

Asked by Erd\H{o}s and Sauer. The prize of \$100 is offered in \cite{Er78} for the case $k=3$ (perhaps just for settling whether the answer is $\ll n$ or not). Resolved by Janzer and Sudakov \cite{JaSu23}, who proved that there exists some $C=C(k)>0$ such that any graph on $n$ vertices with at least $Cn\log\log n$ edges contains a $k$-regular subgraph. Chakraborti, Janzer, Methuku, and Montgomery \cite{CJMM24b} have shown that one can take $C(k)\ll k^2$, which is the best possible up to an absolute constant. A construction due to Pyber, R\"{o}dl, and Szemer\'{e}di \cite{PRS95} shows that this is best possible. In \cite{Er75} Erd\H{o}s mentions a similar question of Szemer\'{e}di, in which the $k$-regular subgraph must be connected. Let $F(n,k)$ be the smallest number of edges on $n$ vertices which guarantee a connected $k$-regular subgraph. Erd\H{o}s \cite{Er75} proved $F(n,3) \ll n^{5/3}$.
